This page documents a cross-language validation snapshot for augmented
balancing experiments. It is self-contained: the displayed results are stored
in this repository. It does not require access to the research directories
where the original R experiments were run.

The estimator is provided by
[crabbymetrics](https://github.com/apoorvalal/crabbymetrics). The related paper
is [Augmented Balancing Estimators of the Average Treatment Effect on the
Treated in Cross-Sectional and Panel
Designs](https://apoorvalal.github.io/files/papers/augbal.pdf).

## Validation question

The check asks whether the Python simulation and estimator pipeline gives Monte
Carlo RMSE values consistent with an earlier R reference grid.

The two languages did not use matched random draws. Therefore, equality cell by
cell is not the correct criterion. For cell $j$, compare

$$
Z_j=
\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{RMSE}}_{P,j}-
      \widehat{\mathrm{RMSE}}_{R,j}}
{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{MCSE}}_{P,j}^2+
       \widehat{\mathrm{MCSE}}_{R,j}^2}}.
$$

Values within a few combined Monte Carlo standard errors are consistent with
simulation noise.

## Included artifacts

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `reference/r_slide_rmse.csv` | R reference RMSE grid |
| `results/python_rmse.csv` | Python RMSE grid |
| `results/r_python_rmse_comparison.csv` | matched comparison with combined MCSE |
| `reference/r_augmented_balancing_panel.csv` | one R-generated panel fixture |
| `reference/r_augmented_balancing_results.csv` | estimator outputs for that fixture |
| `reference/r_outcome_model_panel.csv` | panel used for outcome-model checks |
| `reference/r_outcome_model_surfaces.csv` | R counterfactual surfaces |

The original R project, its package lockfile, and its experiment scripts are
not included. The checked-in R files are reference artifacts, not a complete R
reproduction environment.

## Read the matched grid

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

comparison_path = Path("results/r_python_rmse_comparison.csv")
comparison = pd.read_csv(comparison_path)

print("matched cells:", len(comparison))
print("all keys unique:", not comparison.duplicated(
    ["family", "setting", "frame", "outcome"]
).any())
print("R replications per cell:", sorted(comparison["n_r"].unique()))
print("Python replications per cell:", sorted(comparison["n_python"].unique()))
```

## Main result

```{python}
within_three = int(comparison["within_three_mcse"].sum())
maximum = comparison["standardized_difference"].abs().max()
median = comparison["standardized_difference"].abs().median()

print("cells within three combined MCSE:", within_three)
print("maximum absolute standardized difference:", round(maximum, 3))
print("median absolute standardized difference:", round(median, 3))
```

The comparison contains 398 matched RMSE cells. The stored result shows whether
each Python value is within three combined Monte Carlo standard errors of its R
reference. This is evidence of aggregate distributional agreement. It is not
proof of exact implementation identity.

## Largest discrepancies

```{python}
columns = [
    "family",
    "setting",
    "frame",
    "outcome",
    "r_rmse",
    "python_rmse",
    "standardized_difference",
]

largest = comparison.loc[
    comparison["standardized_difference"].abs().nlargest(8).index,
    columns,
]
print(largest.to_string(index=False))
```

## Visual agreement diagnostics

The left panel compares RMSE values directly. The right panel shows differences
in units of their combined Monte Carlo standard error.

```{python}
#| label: fig-balancing-agreement
#| fig-cap: "R and Python RMSE agreement across 398 matched simulation cells."
#| fig-alt: "A scatter plot compares R and Python RMSE values by design family, and a histogram shows standardized differences."

figure, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5), constrained_layout=True)
families = sorted(comparison["family"].unique())
for family in families:
    selected = comparison["family"] == family
    axes[0].scatter(
        comparison.loc[selected, "r_rmse"],
        comparison.loc[selected, "python_rmse"],
        s=16,
        alpha=0.65,
        label=family.replace("_", " "),
    )
upper = float(comparison[["r_rmse", "python_rmse"]].to_numpy().max())
axes[0].plot((0.0, upper), (0.0, upper), color="black", linestyle="--")
axes[0].set_xlabel("R RMSE")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Python RMSE")
axes[0].set_title("Matched RMSE cells")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7)

axes[1].hist(
    comparison["standardized_difference"],
    bins=np.linspace(-3.0, 3.0, 31),
    color="#3D5A80",
    edgecolor="white",
)
axes[1].axvline(-3.0, color="black", linestyle=":")
axes[1].axvline(3.0, color="black", linestyle=":")
axes[1].set_xlabel("standardized RMSE difference")
axes[1].set_ylabel("matched cells")
axes[1].set_title("Difference relative to combined MCSE")
plt.show()
```

Inspecting the tail is more useful than reporting only an average difference.
It can reveal one outcome model or weighting frame that needs a separate check.

## Rebuild the comparison table

The comparison script uses only the two checked-in RMSE files:

```bash
uv run python -m website.vignettes.balancing_support.compare_r_python
```

It checks that the Python grid has 398 unique keys, joins the R grid on the four
design identifiers, and recomputes differences and combined Monte Carlo
standard errors.

## Rerun the Python Monte Carlo

The Python experiment runner is also included. It requires the optional
`crabbymetrics` estimator source and can be expensive:

```bash
uv sync --extra estimators
uv run python -m website.vignettes.balancing_support.run_balancing_experiments \
  --help
```

Run it only when you intend to refresh the stored Python results. The command
does not reconstruct the absent R environment.

## Interpretation boundary

The snapshot establishes three limited facts:

1. The stored grids have the same 398 design and estimator cells.
2. Their differences can be evaluated relative to Monte Carlo uncertainty.
3. The Python results can be regenerated from the included runner and public
   estimator source.

It does not establish matched random-number parity, reproduce the original R
project from source, or validate every private analysis that used these DGPs.
